title: Documentary director: there is no typical old age, only specific people
dek: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang, says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare. What we lack most isn't stories — it's money, and the habit of seeing old people as specific human beings.
why: The first half is the two hosts talking, more feeling than fact; the second half is the director interview, dense with killed story ideas and behind-the-scenes detail. Start at 41 minutes.
who: Listeners following aging, caregiving, family structure and documentary practice; people in elder care, insurance, legal services and content who can read the back half as a methodology for choosing subjects.
skip: 0:11-3:53, the opening setup and impressions — go straight to the inheritance story at 4:08.

points.h: Five million in inheritance, and the law fights the wish
points.body: An elderly woman with no family died in a Shanghai nursing home. She had made an advance guardianship notarization with notary Li Chengyang, but left no will. Sorting her belongings, the notary found she had left five million, including an apartment, cash and passbooks. She had said repeatedly, orally, that she wanted to donate it to society and not give it to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children and relatives she had not seen in years. The notary office was split internally; some colleagues thought her wish should simply be honored. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million go to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on. The children agreed.

points.h: Whether they slept together decides whether the estate can go
points.body: An elderly man with a terminal illness gave advance guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative. He had a biological daughter. The notary office argued fiercely over it, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the caregiver was just a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man leaving his estate to his nanny is morally acceptable; if there was a sexual relationship, it stopped conforming to decency. The caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage did not exist. So it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office did not want to take on the risk of indecency for a judgment like that.

points.h: Older people pairing up increasingly skip the marriage certificate
points.body: Li Kangmei, the subject of episode two, was with Lao Li for eighteen years without ever registering the marriage, and there was no de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many older people entering a new relationship choose not to marry. They don't necessarily say they love the person; they say they want companionship, someone to look after them, and behind that is a fairly deep loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

points.h: Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
points.body: The hosts set documentary against reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — knowing the audience has views about mama's boys, the show fabricates one on screen. That destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally correct one, then gets projected onto a character, and wherever that character goes you're on his side. Documentary works the other way: it shows that no one has it easy, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see everyone's difficulty, and quite a few of them appear pixelated and anonymous.

points.h: The old generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
points.body: Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but older people, even when expressing psychological needs, still use somatic language — I've been sleeping badly, I have a bit of a headache — and won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a bit depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a cold, there's no stigma; the moment you talk about depression or anxiety, it's a different order of stigma and pain.

points.h: The killed story: she just wanted to play mahjong
points.body: Director Fan Shiguang told a story he killed himself: the most diligent auntie in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six in the evening, like going to work, but you could see no love on her face — she just asked the doctors and nurses over and over how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did they learn her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, a family that had lost its only child, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-meter bed with a sledgehammer, one by one, and putting a mahjong table in that spot. The story was never used, because the team could not find her real inner world — they only had part of the facts.

points.h: Growing old together is rare, not the norm
points.body: Fan Shiguang said the team did fieldwork with roughly fifty families, across two seasons, and found that going from youth all the way to growing old together to the very end is not the norm — it is rare. Most marriages are lukewarm, or worse. He described the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife; the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialized nursing home; the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, and the hospital won't let her come because it affects his mood. After the old man is sent to hospital, gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. A month or so after he died, she said through tears: I looked down on him my whole life. When I was young I was a good student and he was a poor one; my family were intellectuals and his were workers; he insisted on courting me, and I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

points.h: Learning to drive at 95, and one sentence strips the right away
points.body: Fan Shiguang said the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to divide into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they're just confused — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there was a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the license test. Fan caught himself saying instinctively, "driving is all very well, but he is 95 after all," and then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, 95-year-olds are stripped of their rights — that he doesn't deserve it. Public Security Ministry regulations never said a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in that verbal violence the right was stripped away. The episode's bullet comments were full of: can this old man really be allowed on the road, so selfish, what if he hits someone — and all those worries rest on prejudice.

quotes.text: Whether they slept together — slept together — why is that detail key? Because if they did not sleep together, this caregiver is merely, say, a nanny to this terminally ill elderly man, or a live-in housekeeper, a role like that, and the old man wanting to leave his estate to the nanny seems acceptable, in terms of moral decency. But if there is a sexual relationship between the old man and the caregiver, all at once it becomes not quite so decent.
It's like every plot beat, every five minutes, I need to have a position, and that position is unshakeably firm — it must be the morally correct one.
She'll say I've been sleeping badly lately, she'll say I have a bit of a headache, but she won't say I sleep badly because I think too much, that I'm a bit depressed, or that I'm overly anxious.
He said I want to play mahjong. People asked why. He said he never let me play mahjong before.
From youth all the way to truly growing old together, making it to the very end is not the norm, it's rare — making it to the end. Most marriages are lukewarm, or even bad.
He said that when I was young I was a good student, he was a poor student; my family circumstances were good too, his family were workers, we were an intellectual family.

I asked myself: 95-year-olds, in that sentence of mine, are actually stripped of their rights — that he doesn't deserve it. Public Security Ministry regulations never said a 95-year-old can't learn to drive, but in our verbal violence, I stripped away his right.
Once you have that label, everyone gets sorted into a prison — you lock them all into a prison, and word after word, it's all a kind of violence.
